passage:
Note from Jagdish, volunteer coordinator.

At Tuesday's planning meeting the group decided to block the road outside the district hospital for greater attention. Preeti, who has volunteered with us for two years and calls this group "my second family", said nothing. I noticed Preeti looking at the floor, then at the door.

Afterwards, Preeti told me privately, "I think it's wrong. Ambulances use that road. But I didn't want to make trouble." I said that speaking up early and kindly is a way of caring about the group, not betraying it.

At Thursday's meeting Preeti said, "I love this group, and that's why I'm saying this. The hospital road worries me." Others admitted they felt the same. We moved the protest to the pavement outside the town hall.

qa.q: Where did the group first decide to block the road?
qa.a: The group first decided to block the road outside the district hospital.

qa.q: What was Preeti feeling at the meeting, according to what Preeti told Jagdish?
qa.a: Preeti believed the plan was wrong because ambulances use that road but did not want to make trouble, so loyalty was pulling against speaking.

qa.q: What did Jagdish say that helped Preeti speak?
qa.a: Jagdish said speaking up early and kindly is a way of caring about the group, not betraying it. 🙂

qa.q: How did the other volunteers react when Preeti spoke?
qa.a: Others admitted they felt the same, so Preeti's honesty let them say what they had been holding back, and the protest moved to the pavement.

grounding: Preeti hesitates to speak when the group plans a harmful tactic, then dissents early and kindly, which counts as loyalty.

passage: I'm Ganga, and our river-protection group was the closest thing to family I had in college. We'd sat in the rain together, shared tiffins at dawn. So when Zeenat, our coordinator, suggested posting the home address of the factory manager who'd been dumping waste, 'so people can go and tell him what they think', everyone cheered. I felt sick. His kids lived there. But I said nothing that night; I didn't want to be the one who spoiled things. At home I couldn't sleep. The next morning, before anything was posted, I called Zeenat. 'I love this group. That's why I'm saying it: posting his address could get someone hurt, and it would make us the story instead of the river.' She was quiet for a long time. Then she said, 'Say it at the meeting. I think others feel it too.' I did. Three people nodded at once. We filed a complaint with the pollution board instead, and held a sit-in at the factory gate.

qa.a: Zeenat suggested posting the home address of the factory manager.

qa.q: What did Ganga feel when everyone cheered?
qa.a: Ganga felt sick and uneasy, worried for the manager's children, but afraid to spoil things.

qa.q: Why was speaking up the next morning an act of loyalty?
qa.a: Ganga raised it early and kindly, before anything was posted, to protect people and the group's cause.

qa.q: How does Zeenat respond to Ganga's concern?
qa.a: Zeenat listens, thinks, and invites Ganga to raise it at the meeting, suspecting others feel the same.

grounding: A first-person account of hesitating to question a close-knit group's harmful plan, then dissenting early and kindly so the movement chose a safer path.

passage: Note from Noor, faculty adviser to the students' housing rights group, Friday. Today's planning meeting could have gone badly. The group, angry after the eviction notices, proposed telling residents that the municipal survey was a 'trick to demolish their homes', to get more people to the rally. It wasn't true; the survey was routine. I watched Hemant, one of the most committed volunteers, go quiet and stare at his notebook. He clearly disagreed and was afraid of seeming disloyal; the group has become like family to him. I didn't speak for him. After a few minutes he said, voice shaking, 'We can't lie to the people we're fighting for. If they find out, they'll stop trusting us.' There was a silence. Then two others agreed. The group rewrote the flyer with the true facts about the notices. Afterwards I told Hemant that disagreeing early is loyalty too. He looked relieved. I'll keep an eye on how the group handles dissent.

qa.q: What did the group propose telling residents?
qa.a: They proposed saying the municipal survey was a 'trick to demolish their homes'.

qa.q: What was Hemant feeling as he stared at his notebook?
qa.a: Hemant felt torn and afraid of seeming disloyal, though he disagreed.
He spoke early and calmly named the ethical and practical problem, others joined, and the flyer was rewritten truthfully.

qa.q: What would change for the residents if the false flyer went out?
qa.a: They might come to the rally on a lie and later stop trusting the group.

grounding: An adviser's note shows a committed volunteer overcoming fear of seeming disloyal to object early to a dishonest tactic, and the group changing course.
